newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farm ministers hear British BSE progress report.
newsitem.headline: EU farm ministers hear British BSE progress report.

text.p: European Union farm ministers heard a report from Britain on Monday on its progress in fighting mad cow disease but there was no sign of any easing of the worldwide ban on British beef.
The ban was imposed in March after Britain disclosed that the fatal disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), could spread to humans, triggering a massive public health scare.
In June EU leaders agreed a five-point plan for a phased lifting of the embargo depending on Britain implementing a series of strict eradication and control measures.
"We have been very active," British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg told ministers, adding that he would soon put forward a plan to exempt certified BSE-free herds.

Hogg said Britain had moved ahead on four of the five points in the EU agreement, introducing tighter animal feed, slaughter house and cattle processing controls as well as measures to identify and track animal movements.

But he said Britain was waiting for the advice of EU veterinary scientists about the fifth point -- a selective cull of up to 147,000 extra cattle most at risk to BSE -- after a British study claimed the disease could die out in five years.
The cull would be on top of the annual slaughter of one million animals over the age of 30 months.

Hogg said Britain had slaughtered over 900,000 animals, destroying the carcasses. Between 55,000 and 60,000 cattle were now being killed each week and it was expected that 1.2 million animals would be slaughtered by the end of the year.
EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler reiterated that the selective cull was an essential pre-condition for lifting the ban, a Commission official said.
But he added that the speeding up of the main scheme and the prospect of soon clearing the backlog showed that it would soon be possible to carry out the extra cull.
Looking ahead to the next step in easing the crippling ban, Hogg said, "We shall also soon wish to bring forward ideas for a certified herds scheme."
Exemption of certified BSE-free, grass-fed herds could mainly benefit farmers in Northern Ireland where there is a computerised cattle tracking system.
But Hogg told reporters earlier that he was still thinking of a Britain-wide system.

The European Commission, which is fighting off growing allegations at a European Parliament committee of inquiry that it mishandled the BSE crisis, is anxious to be seen to be following scientific advice in any easing of the ban.

Several experts told the committee that a Commission decision on June 11 to ease an embargo on British gelatine -- a beef by-product widely used in food, cosmetics and pharmaceuticals -- was premature.
On Monday, EU scientists said that more research was needed into the transmission of mad cow disease to humans and that meanwhile a ban on British beef by-products, such as gelatine, should remain.

"Whilst the transmission of the BSE agent from animals to humans is becoming more and more probable, it is necessary to evaluate subsequently the risk linked to products from bovine tissues...," said the scientists, headed by Swiss expert Professor Charles Weissmann.
